posts.author: Gunmetal_Dreams
posts.body:
I have been wondering, when does something go from "Inspired by" to "A ripoff of"
The history behind me asking this:
When I first had the idea of doing my own game, I had some idea of what I wanted to base it on, but due to me being graphically challenged, I only had sprites from other games (Phantasy Star II and IV), and planned to use a free RPG making program. I used these to form the ideas to form the characters. Now of course I have RMMZ with a character generator, but I already have the form and the character appearance, weapons (and to some degree personality) hardwired into my story. So it left me wondering, just where is the line crossed?

posts.author: ATT_Turan
posts.body:
When you're inspired by something, you have
elements
of it.
My game is inspired by Final Fantasy V, Final Fantasy Tactics, Suikoden, and Mass Effect - it has a class-changing system where you purchase abilities with points (FF5/Tactics), a collectable cast that stays at a headquarters except those you choose to bring with you (Suikoden) and character relationships that have story and mission effects (Mass Effect).
If my classes were Warrior, Red Mage, Summoner, and Geomancer, my headquarters was in the Dunan Republic, and my characters included Liara and Wrex, now I've gone from elements to including
specific things
from those games and I'm ripping them off.
And yes, of course, actually using any illegally ripped/duplicated assets directly in a game is unquestionably ripping off.

posts.author: Amysaurus
posts.body:
"Inspired by" implies you are intentionally doing something similar to an existing game/property, but allows room for change.
"Ripoff" implies you are intentionally doing something identical or nearly identical to an existing game/property, and also encompasses ripped assets/designs/etc.
In this situation, it's absolutely a ripoff to be using existing character designs and personalities, etc.. It's ultimately up to you whether or not originality is important to you, but it's difficult to make a memorable game when all of its parts are constantly reminding you of something else.

posts.author: ZombieKidzRule
posts.body:
So, I also think it depends on how truly unique the thing is that you are modeling after. I mean with all the tens of thousands of games out there, I would be incredulous if you couldn't find multiple examples of similar looking characters, personalities, etc. that were independently conceived.
The closer you get to duplicating something that is more unique, the more closely you are to ripping off something.
But I have seen way too many examples of people who say this game started this or that game character was the first...only to go...not really. Maybe that was the first time they saw it. But that doesn't mean it was the originator.
I think I have a pretty good moral compass. If I look at what I am doing and I am concerned that it might be stepping over the line of copying or ripping something else off. Then I'm not going to do it.
But again, I would also take a look at what I wanted to do and think to myself, is this really only linked back to this specific origin?
For instance, making a furry, blue, googly-eyed monster that eats cookies and goes Om Nom Nom would be ripping off Sesame Street. But that doesn't mean that every furry, blue monster that likes to eat things ravenously is encroaching on Cookie Monster's territory.
Again, the closer you get to replicating something that is more unique, the more likely you are to cross the line.
And honestly, I would think appearance is much more likely to cause questions than personality. There aren't enough personality types to make every character in every game/story unique.
But that is just my opinion.

posts.author: daMooseNeo
posts.body:
"Inspired By" - You have a lot of elements and veiled references, a lot of familiar touches and feelings, similar mechanics, but its an original production: unique art, sprites, story, etc. If the protagonist in the inspiration is a dark moody character and your character is dark and moody, if each has a wacky sidekick dog, you're still in largely safe territory. The Blizzard "Craft" games (Warcraft, Starcraft) are heavily inspired by the Warhammer and Warhammer 40k franchises and it shows. The Fallout franchise is a "spiritual successor" to the Wasteland franchise. I could make a game about adventuring kids with psychic powers and it would likely wind up a game clearly inspired by Earthbound, but I'd also be steering well clear of the major plot elements and veering left instead of right on ones that do come close.
"Ripping off" - This has its own levels, the most basic and most illegal of which is using direct assets; sprites, music, characters, etc. as well as character likenesses, story and plots, etc. There is a "creative" "ripping off" which is making your production largely identical "with the serial numbers filed off." Pokemon inspires a lot of games that are, technically, unique but are still, really, "ripping off" the franchise even if they aren't expressly cloning Pikachu. That isn't strictly illegal, but could be if too many lines are crossed.
As a final set of elements; you have "Homages", which are often minor elements and thinly veiled references to characters, events, etc. from other materials. If you encounter a wandering amnesiac soldier with a huge sword as a minor character or a relevant NPC in a quest, yea, its Cloud from FF7, but its not really and its not a prominent part of the experience. If you're in a D&D fantasy world and come across a student wizard with a scar on their forehead, its clearly a Harry Potter reference, but it won't cross lines as long as you're not dredging in trademarks and other specific materials. Its just a taste, a fun sample. World of Warcraft is good at this, as well as the next one...
"Parody" has a lot more freedom in terms of look-alike because the whole idea is you're putting on airs of the referenced material but doing something else with it, frequently comedic, which can transform the meaning and the context. Parody is one of the few protected elements of directly repurposing other's work; its how PETA could do a Pokemon flash game about "the abuse" Pokemon "endure." It was parody, made for the purposes of shining a light on perceived injustices using the property to get that point across (it was also brief, stood alone, and not sold, which helps add editorial and public discourse elements to any kind of Fair Use claim). Weird Al is one of the most obvious artists who makes a livelihood out of parody; while he is a gentleman these days about acquiring permission from artists, he is legally in the clear doing what he does and not infringing on the rights of others.
Parody offers the most possibility to actually take something from another creator and use it verbatim, but it treads a fine line in terms of what you're doing with it and how it can be used. You cannot, for instance, replicate an entire game world and make a quasi-sequel and get away with calling it parody.

posts.author: BloodyKun
posts.body:
It's something I struggle with myself whenever I feel inspired by something.  always asking myself, 'Is this not just exactly the same thing?' when looking at some of my ideas.  some are, some aren't, but I find as time goes on ideas will naturally transform and take on a shape more unique to you.  That is, if you don't outright copy/steal something wholesale.  Legally speaking (disclaimer: I'm not a legal consultant or lawyer) it's been a bit interesting to see discourse going on between fans of Pokemon and Palworld, for example.  From what I've seen, they generally play almost entirely differently, but I guess the real snag is trying to find whether a lot of the models were just ripped right from actual Pokemon games and edited.  Really tough to say.  Things like that, I'm sure could get you into hot water fast.  However, things like Yu-gi-oh and Digimon have existed for around just as long, only far less successful, and that tells me its often more about marketshare to these companies than anything else.
As far as ideas go, for another example, Breath of the Wild kind of set some trends for open world adventure games, and others like Immortals Fenyx Rising or Genshin Impact followed suit.  I don't much care for MMOs of any kind but I'd defended the latter early on because while i love Zelda, it shouldn't have a monopoly on basic features that deserve to be spread around rather than held hostage.  That being said, I had no idea gameplay features and mechanics could be patented until Tears of the Kingdom had been revealed for some time...I really don't like the idea of that.
Thing is, probably will be corrected because I may well be wrong, I was under the impression the base assets that come with RPG Maker are fair to use?  I would rather not anyway, but I've seen some being sold that definitely use some if not all.  May not change your own personal definition of what a ripoff is, though.

The gap between Megami Tensei between Pokémon is actually a lot shorter than you might think.  Pokémon creator Saoshi Tajiri pitched the concept of Pokémon to
Nintendo
in 1990, only three years after the release of Digital Devil Story: Megami Tensei.  The game's development took an extremely long time due to various factors such as a lack of manpower & experience as Game Freak had only been formed a year before in 1989 and only had developed one game in that time, a puzzle game for the NES called Quinty (released in the west as
Mendel Palace
).  Development was further slowed down by the fact that Game Freak had to work on other games such as
Yoshi
,
Mario & Wario
, and
Pulseman
in order to pay the bills to continue to fund the development of Pokémon.
Interestingly, the concept of using monsters to fight for you is not only older than both Megami Tensei and Pokémon but also video games as a whole!  The concept was actually popularized in Japanese media by
Capsule Kaijus
from the Ultraseven television series which was cited by Satoshi Tajiri as a major influence on Pokémon.  Capsule monsters have also been referenced in Castlevania: Symphony of the Night in the form of the
Monster Vial
items &
Lufia II: Rise of the Sinistrals
.
The other major influence on Pokémon's core gameplay mechanics & almost certainly other games as well is the traditional pastime of Japanese children catching beetles and making them fight other beetles: [
TV Tropes link
].
Its because of this practice that beetles, usually the Kabutomushi also known as the
Japanese rhinoceros beetle
and the Kuwagatamushi otherwise known as the
Stag beetle
, are so heavily present in Japanese media & associated with combat.
Pokémon for example, features
Pinsir
who is based on a stag beetle &
Heracross
, who is based on the Japanese rhinoceros beetle.
Likewise the Mega Man X series features
Boomer Kuwanger
from the original Mega Man X & his brother
Gravity Beetle
from Mega Man X3.
Yoshimitsu's appearance in Tekken 4 is also based on the Japanese rhinoceros beetle.
And here we have
Beetle
from Kubo And the Two Strings whose appearance is based on the stag beetle.
Its also the reason why the mini-boss
Bugzzy
from the Kirby games gives Kirby the
Suplex
ability when swallowed and why the
Beetle
ability was added in later games.
Hell, the idea of collecting monsters isn't limited to video games either!  In 1990, American toy company Matchbox launched Monster in My Pocket, a series of collectible toy monsters based on monsters from a variety of different sources such as folklore and fiction.
I used to collect these as a kid and use them as monsters in RPG battles that I would act out also using Lego figures as the player characters.
Fun Fact: Its because of Monster in My Pocket that Pokémon is officially called Pokémon outside of Japan.  You see, in Japan the series is officially called ポケットモンスター (Poketto Monsutā) or Pocket Monster with Pokémon being an abbreviated form of the name.  However, they couldn't use the Pocket Monster name outside of Japan because it was deemed to be too similar to Monster in My Pocket, so Nintendo instead decided to use the abbreviated name instead of risk getting sued.

posts.author: ShardsUnremebered40
posts.body:
I see where this thread is going,
I'll say the line is crossed when the lines get too blurry.
Questionable materials (such as your fav. sprite rips imported into character sets)
without any modifications  (such as originfying the art into new collections for remixed content.)
can be considered "stolen/rip-off" [which for free nonprofit fan-games is fine, sort of??]
But, let's say, you had sprite skills, to remix Street Fighter characters, into new creations,
that slightly resemble the originals, but the new colours/palettes, face designs, lay out appearances such as clothes, moves, animation sets, also, set your art works apart from the original. Some may consider this SUPER CHEATING, but also clone pixel arts is yet also a specialty on it's own right. (Can't say I support in total) But it is amazing how many "clone artists" who specializing in remixing sprites or pixel graphics editing can support themselves, for example my brain can think of is just by taking Sonic the Hedgehog transformed into a whole new character (like maybe Bugs Bunny) just by simple re-tracing, manipulating, editing, and re-animating. Though I don't necessarily care for this approach in total because this technique unfortunately came from game piracy practices but however there is also some great remix artists out there who have great talent for it that did came out of it.
I don't know, I mean, the internet is always going to be one of those places where people love the nostalgia of their favorite things to live on forever including their favorite games, movies, and music. So, even with people creating 100% original content with upmost hardwork, secrecy, and other amazing things for their own content. Just remember, the internet will always for legacy archival as long as things like RPG Maker exist will have people upload their 1,000's of Final Fantasy Dragon Quest clones.
So, just think of this. Is your works you publishing for intended Public Retail or Just For Fun?
because clone games unfortunately are kind of intended to be "rip off-ish" as fan celebration to homage the originals but to make money off of it is a questionable practice. Mainly because I don't see hardly anyone going to their favorite game studios such as Square-Enix to get proper licensing or rights of usage permissions or payouts accrediting to the originals behind those materials "borrowed". If you do manage to do so or just a really a somehow sort of slick one, then I  must say good luck to you on that.
